pr_title: Rewrite AtlasEngine to allow arbitrary overhangs
pr_body:
This is practically a from scratch rewrite of AtlasEngine.

The initial approach used a very classic monospace text renderer, where
the viewport is subdivided into cells and each cell is assigned one
glyph texture, just like how real terminals used to work.
While we knew that it would have problems with overly large glyphs,
like those found in less often used languages, we didn't expect the
absolutely massive number of fonts that this approach would break.
For one, the assumption that monospace fonts are actually mostly
monospace has turned out to be a complete lie and we can't force users
to use better designed fonts. But more importantly, we can't just
design an entire Unicode fallback font collection from scratch where
every major glyph is monospace either. This is especially problematic
for vertical overhangs which are extremely difficult to handle in a
way that outperforms the much simpler alternative approach:
Just implementing a bog-standard, modern, quad-based text renderer.

Such an approach is both, less code and runs faster due to a less
complex CPU-side. The text shaping engine (in our case DirectWrite)
has to resolve text into glyph indices anyways, so using them directly
for text rendering allows reduces the effort of turning it back into
text ranges and hashing those. It's memory overhead is also reduced,
because we can now break up long ligatures into their individual glyphs.
Especially on AMD APUs I found this approach to run much faster.

  * Cursor appears correctly

I got a chance to ask someone much more knowledgeable about this today and they suggested to only stop using Direct3D when we don't detect a phyiscal GPU. So I think that's what we'll do now.

But at least in my understanding the current preview builds should already work that way. I'm surprised they don't. If your host has a phyiscal GPU you should always get shader support... 🤔

The new approach doesn't do this, so maybe that's what fixed it.

Okay so, some notes from use.

It's interesting that a renderer error pops up a dialog 3 times, _and then_ triggers the fallback "click here to start rendering again" mechanism.
Resizing it somehow recreates enough resources to make it work again.
That raises the question: why doesn't the "there was a renderer error -20000000" dialog do that?

Can we use the existing fallback failure infrastructure instead of displaying an error dialog? We already have support for it, and it might even _work_. Might. :)

> That raises the question: why doesn't the "there was a renderer error -20000000" dialog do that?

It's a particularly nasty bug... When a new `IBackend` is created we need to ensure to pass a dirty rect that covers the entire viewport. After your comment, I thought about this for quite a while and still couldn't come up with a better alternative than "just make sure to mark everything as dirty".

In the future we should just recreate the entire renderer stack and pass it the existing IRenderData object. Having less setters and callbacks should make this a bit easier hopefully.

@j4james This magnum opus of a Frankensteinian pull request contains an implementation for both line renditions and soft fonts. I'm however entirely stumped on how to integrate the `centeringHint` parameter. If you happen to have time, it would be extremely helpful for me if you help me find a DECDLD sequence that triggers a non-zero `centeringHint`. 😵‍💫 I'd then check the rendering output of `DxRenderer` and match this one's with it.

> @j4james This magnum opus of a Frankensteinian pull request contains an implementation for both line renditions and soft fonts. I'm however entirely stumped on how to integrate the `centeringHint` parameter. If you happen to have time, it would be extremely helpful for me if you help me find a DECDLD sequence that triggers a non-zero `centeringHint`. 😵‍💫 I'd then check the rendering output of `DxRenderer` and match this one's with it.

I couldn't find the original source anymore, but I've uploaded a copy of a VT220 font as a gist here:
https://gist.github.com/j4james/4da454443d8440cadaf84a93f811a35e

Technically it's a set of a `DECDLD` sequences, but if you just `type` or `cat` the file, it'll generate the whole font and immediately map it as as the active character set so you can see what it looks like.

So you know what to look out for, I've output some examples characters below showing the difference between a rendering using the centering hint, and then without the centering hint. It's typically only an issue on vertically symmetric characters, and most noticeable with antialiasing disabled.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/4181424/228986010-5449d07d-c79a-4afb-aacd-ea5a09ca1665.png)

The issue is when you scale the font to make it wider, and you need pick a subset of the source columns to repeat. If the repeated columns aren't evenly balanced on either side of the center point of the glyph, it won't scale symmetrically, and can end up looking a bit lopsided.

The centering hint helps avoid that issue when you've got a font that has an odd width, centered within a cell of an even width, or vice versa. In the example above, the font is 7 pixels wide, centered in a cell that is 10 pixels wide.

Thanks! I've now also been able to reproduce a centering-hint of 1 in my own rendering test application, by setting the sixel width to 14px and getting `FontBuffer` to use the "VT320 - 15x12" path. Unfortunately, (or fortunately?) it seems that I can't find any issues with my rendering approach, even though I'm not making any use of the centering-hint parameter - The glyph size it produces after scaling is identical to what DxRenderer produces, even with various, different soft fonts. I fear I'll only be able to fix a potential flaw in my implementation, if we ever encounter a reproducibly issue with it in the future...

Edit: Ah, I think I get it now. It applies to when you use nearest-neighbor interpolation. Still, however, I'm unable to consistently reproduce an issue and so I'm unsure how to verify a fix for this.

> I fear I'll only be able to fix a potential flaw in my implementation, if we ever encounter a reproducibly issue with it in the future...

If you can't see a problem with your implementation, I wouldn't stress about it for now. Even if there is an issue it probably wouldn't be very noticeable with a high-quality interpolation. This was mostly an optimization for the GDI renderer which can only do nearest-neighbour.

It's worth noting how cursors work on a real terminal, because their way of doing things is dead simple. If it's a block cursor, you toggle the reverse video attribute of the cell, and if it's a underline cursor, you toggle the underline attribute (so if the cell is already underlined, this turns the underline off). A blinking cursor will just flip the attributes on and off.

I'm not positive the color terminals worked the same way, but it seems like a perfectly reasonable solution even in color. There's no scenario in which the cursor makes the text invisible unless it's already invisible. If it was up to me, this would be our default cursor implementation, but I don't think any of our renderers have this as an option.

But if you start with that as the "correct" way to render a cursor, then a red-colored block cursor would render the cell with the background in red, and the text in the original *background* color. And a red underline cursor would render the underline in red, but with the text in the original *foreground* color.

However, to prevent text becoming invisible with a color block cursor, you likely also need to adjust the text color to make sure it always contrasts with the cursor color. And to prevent the underline cursor being invisible when over a matching background color, you'd likely want to adjust the cursor color itself sometimes.

To get this right, you can't think of cursors as just an arbitrary shape that gets rendered in a particular color at a one point in the pipeline. It potentially affects every aspect of the cell's rendering.

After dividing 0xfe01fe01 by 0xff you get 0x00ff00ff again. In other other words, you can multiply R and B by Alpha in a single step and cut the assembly by like a third.
